title: Count the Inversions

concept.title: Count while merging
body: An **inversion** is a pair of positions `i < j` with `a[i] > a[j]`: two elements in the wrong order. Checking all pairs costs O(n^2). Merge sort counts them for free. Sort the left half and the right half (counting their own inversions recursively). Then merge: whenever the next element of the right half is taken **before** the remaining elements of the left half, it is smaller than **all** of them, so it forms an inversion with each.

body.code:
if a[i] <= a[j]:          # take from the left: no new inversion
    tmp[k] = a[i]; i += 1
else:                     # take from the right
    tmp[k] = a[j]; j += 1
    inv += mid - i        # it jumps over all remaining left elements

body: Counting happens during the usual O(n) merge step, so the total work is O(n log n). Use 64-bit numbers for the count: for 20000 elements it can reach about 2 * 10^8, and in general it is as large as `n * (n - 1) / 2`.

statement: Count the pairs of positions `i < j` with `a[i] > a[j]` in an array of `n` integers.
hints: Counting all pairs is O(n^2); think of merge sort.
When merging two sorted halves, an element taken from the right half is smaller than every element still waiting in the left half.
Add the number of waiting left elements (`mid - i`) to the answer at that moment.

explanation: Merge sort splits the array, counts the inversions inside each half, and counts the pairs that cross the middle during the merge: every element taken from the right half forms an inversion with all waiting left elements.
solution.complexity: Time O(n log n), space O(n).

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

def merge_count(a, tmp, lo, hi):
    if hi - lo <= 1:
        return 0
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    inv = merge_count(a, tmp, lo, mid) + merge_count(a, tmp, mid, hi)
    i, j, k = lo, mid, lo
    while i < mid and j < hi:
        if a[i] <= a[j]:
            tmp[k] = a[i]
            i += 1
        else:
            tmp[k] = a[j]
            j += 1
            inv += mid - i
        k += 1
    while i < mid:
        tmp[k] = a[i]
        i += 1
        k += 1
    while j < hi:
        tmp[k] = a[j]
        j += 1
        k += 1
    a[lo:hi] = tmp[lo:hi]
    return inv

n = int(input())
a = list(map(int, input().split()))

tmp = [0] * n
print(merge_count(a, tmp, 0, n))
